TypeScript - write a generic withTimeout(promise, ms, label) that rejects if the promise doesn't settle in time (the core, no imports).
What's the SHAPE of a promise timeout (to reconstruct withTimeout)?
column2:
Promise.race([ theRealPromise, aNewPromise<never> that setTimeout(...)s a reject after ms ]).
Settles with whichever finishes first: the real value, or the timeout's rejection.
Type the timeout promise <never> since it only ever rejects.

column1: SOCKS proxy - socks5:// vs socks5h://, and which bypasses a client-side DNS block?
column2:
socks5:// resolves the hostname CLIENT-side, then connects through the proxy.
socks5h:// makes the PROXY do the DNS.
If the client's network blocks DNS for the target (e.g. Telegram from Russia), use socks5h -
then lookup + connection both happen at the proxy; the client only needs the proxy's IP.

column1: grammY - route new Bot() through a SOCKS5 proxy ONLY when a proxy URL is set (inert otherwise).
A bot in a blocked region can't reach an external API. Smallest fix without a full VPN/tunnel?
column2:
Point the HTTP client at a SOCKS5 proxy on a VPS in an unblocked region
(grammY: client.baseFetchConfig.agent = new SocksProxyAgent(url)).
Only that app's traffic is routed; no container-level routing/tunnel needed.
Use socks5h so DNS happens at the proxy. Gate on an env var so it stays inert where the API is reachable.

column1: curl - what does -x do, and how does it differ from -X?
column2:
-x (lowercase) = --proxy: route the request THROUGH a proxy
  (e.g. -x socks5h://user:pass@ip:1080).
-X (uppercase) = --request: set the HTTP method (-X POST).
One letter apart, completely different.

column1: Env files - when does a var belong in .env.production vs the base .env?
column2:
.env.production is for OVERRIDES - vars whose VALUE differs by environment
(e.g. DATABASE_URL host: localhost vs postgres:5432).
A var simply absent in dev and present in prod (e.g. TELEGRAM_PROXY) is NOT an override -
put it in the base .env (the file actually loaded), empty locally.
First confirm which file the runtime reads (dotenv loads .env by default, not .env.production).

column1: You add a prod-only env var but the app doesn't pick it up. First thing to verify?
column2:
Which env file the runtime actually LOADS. dotenv loads .env by default, not .env.production,
unless explicitly pointed at it. Confirm with:
  exec <svc> sh -c 'echo ${VAR:+set}'
checks the process environment directly. If empty, the var is in a file the app never reads.

column1: Zod - a generic helper mapping a blank/whitespace env string to undefined BEFORE the inner schema runs.
Zod - why does z.coerce.number().optional() turn an empty env string into 0, and the fix?
column2:
coerce runs FIRST (Number("") === 0), before .optional() sees the value -
so "" becomes 0 and .optional() never fires.
Fix: z.preprocess maps "" -> undefined BEFORE coercion, restoring the meaning of "absent"
so .optional() and .refine() work.

column1: Zod - preprocess vs transform: which runs when, and which cleans a blank env var?
column2:
preprocess runs BEFORE validation (input unknown) - use it to CLEAN input (blank -> undefined).
transform runs AFTER validation - use it to RESHAPE a valid value.
For a blank env var: preprocess, so the cleaned value is what gets validated.

column1: Zod - the .transform().pipe() equivalent of preprocess, and the one gotcha?
column2:
z.unknown().transform(clean).pipe(schema) - transform's OUTPUT feeds pipe's schema as input
(like cat | grep). Gotcha: a block-body arrow (val) => { ... } with no return returns undefined -
you MUST explicitly return val for the pass-through case.
preprocess reads clearer for cleaning; pipe shines when both stages are real schemas.

Prisma - why prefer updateMany over update to revoke one row in a many-to-many join by a far-side name?
column2:
update needs the composite key (userId_roleId) and THROWS P2025 if the row doesn't exist.
updateMany filters via the relation (role: { name: MANAGER }), needs no separate role lookup,
returns { count } instead of throwing, and lets you guard with revokedAt: null.
count tells you whether anything changed.

Prisma - a chatId lookup returns null for a row you KNOW exists. First thing to check?
column2:
Whether the column is BigInt and you passed a raw number. Wrap it: where: { chatId: BigInt(chatId) }.
A number-vs-BigInt mismatch matches nothing silently - the classic 'can't find an existing row' cause.

column1: Prisma - top-level where vs a where nested inside select?
column2:
Top-level where decides WHETHER THE PARENT ROW returns.
A nested where (inside select/include) filters WHICH CHILDREN come back - it does NOT gate the parent.
some/none/every in a top-level where gate the PARENT by its children.

TypeScript - .includes("*") on a tuple-union errors with 'not assignable to never'. Why, and fix?
column2:
as const makes each permissions a readonly tuple of literals; the union's .includes arg type is
the INTERSECTION of all tuples = never. Fix: flatten first, then filter element-by-element -
.flatMap(r => r.permissions).filter(p => p !== "*") - so you operate on individual strings.

Git - undo a PUSHED commit vs a LOCAL one. Which tool for each?
column2:
Pushed: git revert <commit> - NEW inverse commit, preserves history, safe to share.
Local-only: git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard HEAD~1 - moves the pointer, rewrites history.
Rule: pushed -> revert, local -> reset.

column1: Git reset - what do --soft, --mixed, --hard each keep or discard?
column2:
--soft HEAD~1: undo commit, changes stay STAGED.
--mixed (default): undo commit, changes kept but UNSTAGED.
--hard: undo commit AND discard the changes (destructive).
Only --hard loses work.

column1: Git - discard uncommitted edits to a file, and unstage a file keeping its edits.
column2:
Discard working-tree edits: git restore <file>.
Unstage but keep edits: git restore --staged <file>.
(restore replaced the old confusing "checkout -- <file>" / "reset HEAD <file>".)

column1: Prisma - how do you undo a schema change in production, and why is dropping a table special?
column2:
Migrations are forward-only (no auto 'down') - write a NEW migration that reverses it (like git revert).
NEVER prisma migrate reset in prod (drops the whole DB).
Dropping a table is irreversible for the DATA - rows are gone even if you re-add the table.
So before a drop, the undo is a BACKUP (pg_dump), not a migration.

column1: When does dropping a table CASCADE into data in a table you meant to keep?
column2:
When a table you KEEP has an onDelete: Cascade FK pointing AT the table you're dropping -
deleting the parent cascades into the kept child. FKs pointing OUTWARD from the dropped table
are harmless (they vanish with it). Safe design: log/snapshot tables store a plain denormalized
value (e.g. managerChatId BigInt, NO @relation) so dropping the entity can't touch the log.

column1: yarn db:migrate --name foo fails with 'unknown option --name'. Why, and the fix?
column2:
The script is "prisma migrate dev && prisma generate" - yarn appends --name to the TAIL command
(prisma generate), which doesn't know it. migrate already succeeded; only the chained generate errors.
Fix: split the scripts so --name reaches migrate alone -
  "db:migrate": "prisma migrate dev",  "db:generate": "prisma generate"

column1: Ops - container is Up, process alive, env injected, but logs stop after one line, no crash/stacktrace. What class of failure?
column2:
A HANG on an await to an unreachable external host - not a crash.
A crash leaves a stack trace; silence after startup = a promise that never resolves
(e.g. bot.init() calling a blocked API). Confirm reachability from inside the container before touching code.

column1: Resilience - an external call can hang forever with no log. How to make the failure diagnosable?
column2:
Race it against a timeout (withTimeout / Promise.race) so it rejects with a LOGGED error
and exits non-zero (container restarts) instead of becoming a silent zombie.
Mitigates the symptom; does NOT fix the underlying reachability.

column1: RBAC - the 'cannot remove yourself' rule: what's the environment-agnostic invariant that beats gating on NODE_ENV?
column2:
A count check: "would this leave zero active admins?" - environment-agnostic, runs everywhere,
and expresses the REAL rule (don't lock everyone out).
Gating "is this self?" on NODE_ENV === "production" means the rule never runs in dev,
so it can break unseen. The self-check is a proxy; the count is the actual invariant.

column1: RBAC - implement 'would this leave zero active admins?' as a count guard (shape).
column2:
Before revoking: count active assignments of the critical role
(prisma.userRole.count where revokedAt: null, role.name = ADMIN/MANAGER, user.isActive: true).
If removing this one would drop the count to 0, refuse. Same gate shape as the seed bootstrap.
